title: Generic graded initial ideals are fixed by triangular substitutions
statement: Let $L$ be a field of characteristic zero [def-weil-field], let $n\ge0$, and let $J\subset L[T_1,\ldots,T_n]$ be a homogeneous ideal [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring], meaning that every homogeneous component of any element of $J$ lies in $J$. In each fixed degree order exponents lexicographically by $(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)$, taking the least exponent of a nonzero polynomial. For a homogeneous ideal $H$, let $\operatorname{in}_{\min}(H)$ be the monomial ideal generated by those least monomials of its homogeneous elements. There exist a nonempty Zariski open subset $\Omega\subset\operatorname{GL}_n(L)$ and one monomial ideal $B$ such that $\operatorname{in}_{\min}(gJ)=B$ for every $g\in\Omega$, where $g$ acts by linear substitution. Here open means the intersection with $\operatorname{GL}_n$ of a Zariski open in the affine space of matrices, and nonempty means geometrically nonempty. The ideal $B$ is invariant under each substitution $T_i\mapsto T_i+\lambda T_j$, $T_h\mapsto T_h$ for $h\ne i$, whenever $i<j$ and $\lambda\in L$.

source.place: Generic-coordinate input recalled in BM 1997, section 8 and before Theorem 9.6, printed pp.273 and 278. Graded form: Galligo--Bayer--Stillman theorem; Bayer--Stillman, A theorem on refining division orders by the reverse lexicographic order, Duke Math. J. 55 (1987), Proposition 1. The variable-reversed graded reverse lexicographic convention gives the least fixed-degree lexicographic monomial used here. This supporting paper is WANTED; no Stacks tag states generic Borel fixity.

proof.text: If $n=0$, the polynomial ring is $L$, so its only ideals are $0$ and $L$: a nonzero member of an ideal is a unit. For any $n$, the ideals $J=0$ and $J=L[T]$ already have constant initial ideals $0$ and $L[T]$ under all invertible substitutions. Take $\Omega=\operatorname{GL}_n$ and that initial ideal in these cases; the required invariance is immediate. Henceforth assume $n\ge1$ and $J$ is nonzero and proper. Write $P_q$ for the space with the finite basis of degree-$q$ monomials, ordered by increasing lexicographic exponent, and $J_q=J\cap P_q$.

source.place: VIII 2.3.13, printed p.94, supplies the resolution context only; Q86 agent proof of the missing generic-coordinate input: zero-variable, zero-ideal and unit-ideal cases; finite monomial bases

proof.text: Here is the finite linear calculation used below, over any field $F$. For a subspace $W\subset F^N$ with its ordered coordinate basis, eliminate the leftmost nonzero column, normalize its pivot, eliminate that column from other rows, and repeat on the remaining rows. This produces a basis $f_\alpha=e_\alpha+\sum_{\beta>\alpha,\ \beta\notin S}c_{\alpha\beta}e_\beta$ indexed by a set $S$ of pivot columns. In a nonzero linear combination, the smallest pivot whose coefficient is nonzero is the first nonzero coordinate. Thus the possible first coordinates of members of $W\setminus0$ are exactly $S$, and $|S|=\dim W$. The process terminates after at most $N$ pivots; the pivot coefficients determine the coefficients of each linear combination uniquely.

source.place: VIII 2.3.13, printed p.94, supplies the resolution context only; Q86 agent proof of the missing generic-coordinate input: explicit row elimination and its first-coordinate description

proof.text: For a homogeneous ideal $H\subset F[T]$, let $D(H)$ be the exponents of the least monomials of its nonzero homogeneous elements. If $\alpha\in D(H)$, multiplication of a witnessing polynomial by $T^\gamma$ shows $\alpha+\gamma\in D(H)$: lexicographic comparison is unchanged by adding $\gamma$. Consequently the monomial ideal generated by these least monomials is precisely the $F$-linear span of $T^\alpha$ for $\alpha\in D(H)$. Indeed a product of a polynomial and a generating monomial expands into monomials in that upward-closed set, and every monomial in the set is a generator. Its degree-$q$ basis is therefore the pivot set of $H_q$ from step 2. In particular its degree-$q$ dimension equals $\dim_F H_q$.

source.place: VIII 2.3.13, printed p.94, supplies the resolution context only; Q86 agent proof of the missing generic-coordinate input: coefficientwise description of the initial ideal and equality of degree dimensions

proof.text: Introduce independent matrix entries $z_{ab}$, put $K=L(z_{ab})$ (fractions of polynomials in these entries), and let $G=(z_{ab})$. Its determinant is a nonzero polynomial, since its diagonal monomial has coefficient $1$, so the adjugate divided by that determinant gives its inverse over $K$. Extend each $J_q$ to its $K$-linear span, and put $H=GJ_K$. The sum of these spans is an ideal: multiplying by a monomial carries $J_q$ into the appropriate $J_{q+|\gamma|}$. Substitution by $G$ is an automorphism preserving degree, so $\dim_K H_q=\dim_L J_q$. The set $D=D(H)$ is upward closed by step 3. Apply [lem-trf-monomial-upper-set-finite-basis] to $D$: its componentwise minimal elements form an antichain, hence a finite set $A$, and every element of $D$ dominates an element of $A$. Thus $D=\bigcup_{\alpha\in A}(\alpha+\mathbf N^n)$. Let $B\subset L[T]$ be the monomial ideal generated by $T^\alpha$, $\alpha\in A$. Its extension to $K$ is $\operatorname{in}_{\min}(H)$.

source.place: VIII 2.3.13, printed p.94, supplies the resolution context only; Q86 agent proof of the missing generic-coordinate input: generic matrix; finite minimal exponents from Dickson finiteness and minimal domination

proof.text: For each $\alpha\in A$, choose a homogeneous $f_\alpha\in H_{|\alpha|}$ with least monomial $T^\alpha$, normalized to coefficient $1$. Choose an $L$-basis $p_{\alpha,1},\ldots,p_{\alpha,r_\alpha}$ of $J_{|\alpha|}$. Express $f_\alpha=\sum_\ell c_{\alpha\ell}(z)G p_{\alpha,\ell}$ over $K$. Let $d_\alpha(z)$ be a nonzero common polynomial denominator for this finite list of rational coefficients, and let $Q(z)=\det(z)\prod_{\alpha\in A}d_\alpha(z)$. Define $\Omega$ by $Q\ne0$. This is the intersection of an affine principal open with $\operatorname{GL}_n$. The polynomial $Q$ is nonzero: in a polynomial ring over a field the lexicographically greatest nonzero term of a product is the product of the greatest terms, with nonzero coefficient. Hence $\Omega$ is geometrically nonempty; after extension to an algebraic closure, a nonzero polynomial cannot vanish at every tuple, by induction on its number of variables and the one-variable root bound.

source.place: VIII 2.3.13, printed p.94, supplies the resolution context only; Q86 agent proof of the missing generic-coordinate input: finite denominator open, not an infinite intersection of degreewise opens

proof.text: Let $F/L$ be any field extension and $g\in\Omega(F)$. Evaluating the finite expressions in step 5 gives polynomials $f_\alpha(g)\in(gJ_F)_{|\alpha|}$ whose coefficients before $\alpha$ are $0$ and whose coefficient at $\alpha$ is $1$, because these were rational-function identities with allowed denominators. Thus $B_F\subset\operatorname{in}_{\min}(gJ_F)$. In degree $q$, both spaces have dimension $\dim_L J_q$: for $B_F$ use its fixed monomial basis and steps 3--4, and for the other space use step 3 and the invertibility of $g$. An inclusion of finite-dimensional spaces of equal dimension is equality (extend a basis of the smaller space). Equality in every degree gives $B_F=\operatorname{in}_{\min}(gJ_F)$. This proves the required simultaneous stabilization in all degrees, including over $F=L$.

source.place: VIII 2.3.13, printed p.94, supplies the resolution context only; Q86 agent proof of the missing generic-coordinate input: specialization, inclusion of monomial ideals and degreewise dimension comparison

proof.text: Choose $g_0\in\Omega(L)$. Such a point exists since characteristic zero makes $L$ infinite: the elements $m\cdot1$, $m\ge0$, are distinct. For completeness, a nonzero polynomial over an infinite field has a nonvanishing value: write it as a polynomial in the last variable, choose values of the preceding variables at which a nonzero coefficient stays nonzero by induction, and then avoid the finitely many roots in the last variable. The one-variable bound follows by repeatedly dividing by $X-a$ at a root, reducing the degree. Apply this to $Q$. Fix a degree $q\ge1$, and let $S$ be the degree-$q$ monomial basis of $B_q$. By step 6 it is the pivot set of $(g_0J)_q$. If $S$ is empty, $B_q=0$ is already invariant. Suppose it has size $r>0$.

source.place: VIII 2.3.13, printed p.94, supplies the resolution context only; Q86 agent proof of the missing generic-coordinate input: rational point in the generic open; reduction to one nonzero degree space

proof.text: Choose an $L$-basis $p_1,\ldots,p_r$ of $J_q$, and let $M(z)$ be the $r\times\dim P_q$ matrix whose rows are the coefficients of $Gp_\ell$. Its entries are polynomials in $z$. The square submatrix $M_S(g_0)$ is invertible since $S$ is the pivot set. Put $R(z)=M_S(z)^{-1}M(z)$; its entries are rational functions with denominators powers of $\det M_S(z)$, nonvanishing at $g_0$. Over $K$ the pivot set is also $S$ by steps 3--4, so $R(z)$ is exactly the normalized pivot basis from step 2. Its row indexed by $\alpha\in S$ is $T^\alpha+\sum_{\beta>\alpha,\ \beta\notin S}c_{\alpha\beta}(z)T^\beta$. In particular the zero entries before each pivot are rational-function identities, not assertions holding merely at $g_0$.

source.place: VIII 2.3.13, printed p.94, supplies the resolution context only; Q86 agent proof of the missing generic-coordinate input: one pivot minor gives rational normalized rows regular at the chosen point

proof.text: Fix $i<j$ and $\lambda\in L$, and write $b(T_i)=T_i+\lambda T_j$, $b(T_h)=T_h$ for $h\ne i$. Choose $w_h=(q+1)^{n-h}$. On degree-$q$ exponents the number $w\cdot\alpha$ strictly increases with lexicographic order: at the first differing index the contribution $(q+1)^{n-h}$ exceeds the total possible contribution $q\sum_{k>h}(q+1)^{n-k}=(q+1)^{n-h}-1$ of later indices. Define $\tau(t)(T_h)=t^{w_h}T_h$ over $L(t)$ and $h(t)=\tau(t)^{-1}b\tau(t)g_0$, with products denoting composition of substitutions. Direct substitution gives $\tau^{-1}b\tau(T_i)=T_i+\lambda t^{w_i-w_j}T_j$ and fixes the other variables. Since $w_i>w_j$, the entries of $h(t)$ are polynomials in $t$ and $h(0)=g_0$. Thus every denominator in $R(h(t))$ has nonzero value at $0$.

source.place: VIII 2.3.13, printed p.94, supplies the resolution context only; Q86 agent proof of the missing generic-coordinate input: finite-degree lex weights and explicit conjugation formula fixing the triangular direction

proof.text: Let $\mathcal O=\{a(t)/d(t)\in L(t):a,d\in L[t],\ d(0)\ne0\}$, with reduction $a/d\mapsto a(0)/d(0)$. Substitute $h(t)$ into the rows of $R$, obtaining $f_\alpha(t)=T^\alpha+\sum_{\beta>\alpha,\ \beta\notin S}c_{\alpha\beta}(h(t))T^\beta$. The coefficients lie in $\mathcal O$ by step 9. The polynomials $F_\alpha(t)=t^{-w\cdot\alpha}\tau(t)f_\alpha(t)$ also have coefficients in $\mathcal O$: each tail coefficient has the extra positive power $t^{w\cdot\beta-w\cdot\alpha}$. Their reductions are exactly $T^\alpha$, $\alpha\in S$, and they form a basis over $L(t)$ of $(\tau(t)h(t)J_{L(t)})_q$. Similarly, applying the same scaling to the fixed rows $f^0_\alpha=R(g_0)_\alpha$ gives $E_\alpha(t)=t^{-w\cdot\alpha}\tau(t)f^0_\alpha$ with coefficients in $L[t]$ and reduction $T^\alpha$. The rows $bE_\alpha(t)$ have reduction $bT^\alpha$ and span $(b\tau(t)g_0J_{L(t)})_q$. These two row spaces over $L(t)$ coincide, because $\tau(t)h(t)=b\tau(t)g_0$.

source.place: VIII 2.3.13, printed p.94, supplies the resolution context only; Q86 agent proof of the missing generic-coordinate input: explicit scaled row bases; no flat-family or Grassmannian-limit theorem used

proof.text: Compare the two bases in step 10 by coefficients rather than by an assumed uniqueness of limits. Let $U$ be the matrix of the rows $F_\alpha(t)$ and $V$ the matrix of the rows $bE_\alpha(t)$. They have coefficients in $\mathcal O$ and the same row space over $L(t)$, so $U=CV$ for an invertible $r\times r$ matrix over $L(t)$. The reductions of the rows of $V$ are independent, since $b$ is invertible and the $T^\alpha$ are independent. Choose $r$ columns $I$ for which $V_I(0)$ is invertible; then $C=U_I V_I^{-1}$ has entries in $\mathcal O$, by the adjugate formula and $\det V_I(0)\ne0$. Reducing $U=CV$ gives $B_q\subset bB_q$. Both spaces have dimension $r$, so $B_q=bB_q$. This is the complete specialization comparison in this argument.

source.place: VIII 2.3.13, printed p.94, supplies the resolution context only; Q86 agent proof of the missing generic-coordinate input: unit-minor coefficient comparison proves equality of the two reduced subspaces

proof.text: The calculation in steps 7--11 applies separately to every $q\ge1$ and to each chosen $i<j$ and $\lambda$. Degree zero is zero since $J$ is proper, by step 3 (and was already covered for the unit ideal in step 1). As $b$ preserves degree and $B$ is the direct sum of its monomial degree spaces, $bB_q=B_q$ for all $q$ implies $bB=B$. Together with the single geometrically nonempty open $\Omega$ from steps 5--6, this is every assertion of the item. The diagonal weights may depend on $q$; the open $\Omega$ and the ideal $B$ do not.

lean.statement: theorem gradedGenericInitialBorel {L : Type u} [Field L] [CharZero L] (n : ℕ) (J : Ideal (MvPolynomial (Fin n) L)) (hJ : ∀ p ∈ J, ∀ q : ℕ, homogeneousComponent q p ∈ J) : ∃ (U : TopologicalSpace.Opens (PrimeSpectrum (MvPolynomial (Fin n × Fin n) L))) (B : Ideal (MvPolynomial (Fin n) L)), (∃ S : Set (Fin n →₀ ℕ), B = Ideal.span ((fun α : Fin n →₀ ℕ ↦ monomial α (1 : L)) '' S)) ∧ (∃ g : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) (AlgebraicClosure L), g.det ≠ 0 ∧ pointToPoint (k := L) (fun ij : Fin n × Fin n ↦ g ij.1 ij.2) ∈ U) ∧ (∀ g : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) L, g.det ≠ 0 → pointToPoint (k := L) (fun ij : Fin n × Fin n ↦ g ij.1 ij.2) ∈ U → gradedLexInitialIdeal (J.map (aeval (fun i ↦ ∑ j : Fin n, C (g i j) * X j)).toRingHom) = B) ∧ ∀ (i j : Fin n), i < j → ∀ c : L, B.map (aeval (fun h : Fin n ↦ if h = i then X i + C c * X j else X h)).toRingHom = B
